head:
Children · Endurance

Has children's endurance declined, and what does it mean for their future?

You often hear that children run less well than their parents did at the same age. That is true on average, but the reality is more nuanced than the slogan: the decline was clear in the 1980s and 1990s, then it almost stopped. What this decline means for a child's future is even more uncertain than press headlines suggest. This article moves step by step, from the most general to the most precise, and ends with an answer and with what you can do.

The question

A 10-year-old who gets out of breath after two minutes of running is nothing unusual. Millions of children in that situation would be a public health issue, provided it is true: that it is more common than before, and that it has consequences. Yet spectacular figures circulate on this subject, such as "25% of cardiovascular capacity lost in forty years", whose origin cannot be found. So there are two opposite risks: downplaying a real problem, or panicking over a figure that does not exist.

To settle it, you need to separate three questions that are not equally solid. The first is an observation: is children's measured endurance lower than before? The second is a measurement: by how much, for whom, and when? The third is a consequence: does this compromise their health as adults, or is it a simple change of level with no effect? The answers do not carry the same degree of evidence, and that is what makes the subject interesting.

The question

Has children's endurance declined, by how much, and does it change anything for their future?

The reasoning follows six steps, each going one notch further into the detail:

  1. Can a child's endurance be measured? Without that, everything else rests on nothing.
  2. What do 33 years of measurements around the world show? The general finding.
  3. Who is affected, where and at what age? The countries, France, girls and boys, adolescence.
  4. Why? The causes put forward, and what has not been demonstrated.
  5. Why does it matter for what comes next? What childhood endurance foretells for the adult.
  6. And what if we are wrong? The objections, what remains uncertain.

What is at stake

The endurance in question is the ability of the heart, lungs and muscles to produce energy using oxygen, and therefore to sustain an effort. In the laboratory it is measured by VO2max, the maximum amount of oxygen the body uses per minute and per kilo. In adults, it is one of the best known markers of heart health. In a cohort of 122,007 patients tested on a treadmill, the highest-fitness group had an 80% lower risk of death than the lowest group, and a low level weighed at least as much as smoking.11 These are associations observed in patients, not proof of cause: we will come back to this, because step 6 qualifies their scope.

For a child, three things are at stake. The first is long-term health: in 2020 the American Heart Association proposed treating endurance as a vital sign in young people, because it is linked, according to the press report of this statement, to cardiometabolic health, mental health and school results.12 The second is the starting point: a child who gets out of breath quickly more easily avoids the activities that would help them improve. This is a reasonable hypothesis, which the studies read here do not test. The third is collective: if the average level of a whole generation falls, health services and schools will see it before families feel it.

Why not leave the question unanswered? Because a child is rarely measured, and nobody warns them when their level is low. And because a mistake costs in both directions: ignoring a real decline delays useful action, while shouting about a false one distracts from what is established. So we have to start from what the measurements actually show.

Step 1 of 6
rest:
Can a child's endurance be measured?

What is claimed: yes, but only in a group. The laboratory requires a mask, a gas analyser and a supervised maximal effort, which is impossible with thousands of pupils. Population studies therefore use the 20-metre shuttle run: the child runs from one line to the other at the pace of a sound signal that speeds up, in one-minute stages, until they can no longer keep up. The speed of the last completed stage is recorded. An equation, which takes age into account, converts it into an estimated VO2max.1

Is this estimate reliable? A meta-analysis of 57 studies finds a correlation of 0.78 (95% confidence interval: 0.72 to 0.85) between the shuttle run score and measured VO2max in children, against 0.94 in adults. The closer the correlation is to 1, the more the test ranks people the way the laboratory does. The authors conclude that, in children, the score alone is a weaker estimator and should be combined with other variables, and that the result remains an estimate, not a direct measurement.6 In the main study we are going to use, the equation has a standard error of 5.9 mL/kg/min (12.1%) in a Quebec sample.1

What this means

The error of the equation (5.9) is larger than the average decline we are about to discuss (3.3). For a single child, this test therefore does not allow much to be concluded about their VO2max. It works for comparing groups: the same error applies to every year and cancels out when numbers are large. Everything that follows is about groups, never about one particular child.

The next question is therefore: what do these group comparisons show when they are put end to end?

Step 2 of 6

What do 33 years of measurements around the world show?

What is claimed: yes, estimated endurance has declined, moderately, mostly before 2000. The largest analysis brings together 137 studies and 965,264 young people aged 9 to 17, in 19 countries (17 high-income, 2 upper-middle-income), tested between 1981 and 2014. Estimated VO2max falls by 3.3 mL/kg/min on average, or 7.3% (95% confidence interval: 7.8 to 6.7%).1

What does 7.3% represent? The two figures give, by a simple calculation, a starting level of about 45 mL/kg/min for the 1981 group. A loss of 3.3 sits just below 3.5, the unit (one "MET") that researchers use to express how much an adult's endurance matters: the authors point out that such a difference in adults is associated with 13% more risk of death from all causes.1 They describe the decline in young people as moderate, but say they see in it a possible sign of a significant setback in population health. This link is their interpretation, not a result of their study.

The decisive point is the pace. Splitting the period by decade shows that the loss was concentrated at the beginning.

The decline has lost almost all its speed since the 2000s

Estimated VO2max loss per decade, 19 countries, 965,264 young people aged 9 to 17 (loss values, sign reversed for readability). Effect descriptors given by the authors; the last confidence interval (2010) runs from -0.4 to 0.0. Source: Tomkinson et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2019.1

What this means

Today's children are not collapsing: most of the loss dates from the 1980s and 1990s, and the authors note a stabilisation close to zero around 2000. But nobody has made up for what was lost. Today's child therefore starts from a lower average level than a generation ago, without families having been told.

A nuance on dates: a review of 22 studies (ages 6 to 18, from 1972 to 2015) first describes a rise in endurance until about 1986, then a decline until 2010-2012, with a slowdown after 2000 and, since 2010, a stabilisation or slight improvement. The authors point out that endurance is the fitness component that has varied the most, and that the differences in protocol between studies are largest for it.5 Choosing 1981 as the starting point therefore means looking at the decline from a possibly high level. This world average nevertheless hides large differences, which we now look at.

Step 3 of 6

Who is affected, where, and at what age?

What is claimed: the decline is widespread but uneven, and more marked in boys and in adolescents. Of the 19 countries, 17 saw a decline. Brazil and Japan record small increases. The largest declines concern Australia, Canada, France, Hungary, Lithuania, Poland and the Seychelles. In Belgium, the decline even turned into an increase, and the United Kingdom followed the opposite path. By sex, the decline is large in boys and small in girls. These 19 countries represent about 15% of the world's population: we do not know what is happening elsewhere.1

The case of France

An analysis of 15,420 French young people aged 9 to 16, tested with the shuttle run between 1999 and 2022, gives a very clear picture. The researchers adjusted the results for protocol, age, sex and body mass index, then expressed them in standard deviations, that is, relative to the usual spread of results. Before 2010, average performance loses 2.31 standard deviations per decade. Losing more than two standard deviations in ten years is a very large shift in how children rank compared with previous generations. After 2010, the loss falls to 0.15 standard deviation per decade, about 0.06 times the previous rate. The authors speak of a considerable slowdown, while asking for more data to confirm it.2

In France, the decline has almost stopped since 2010

15,420 young people aged 9 to 16, 1999 to 2022, results adjusted for protocol, age, sex and body mass index. Breakpoint estimated at 2010. 95% confidence intervals: -2.39 to -2.24 before 2010, -0.20 to -0.10 after. Source: Vanhelst et al., Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports, 2024 (abstract).2

What this means

Two pieces of information for a French family. The decline is real and large over the 1999-2010 period, and it is not explained by weight alone, since BMI is adjusted for. It then almost stopped. The authors also note that the best performers (above the 75th percentile) fall back a little less than the others: the average therefore hides differences between children.

Age and sex: the example of Quebec

A third study allows a close look at age. In 2014-2017 it repeated the same shuttle run as in 1982, in the same region, with 3,725 pupils aged 6 to 17 in 36 schools across six Quebec cities. Comparing two generations with the same test and the same region avoids many pitfalls.3

The gap with the 1982 generation is larger in adolescents

Scale: 8 px per percentage point, starting from zero. A single province, cross-sectional comparison (different pupils in each period). Source: Leone et al., Frontiers in Public Health, 2023.3

What this means

At age 6, the gap with 1982 is already there, around 8%. At age 17, it is about 2.3 times larger for boys (17.7 versus 7.6) and about 1.5 times for girls (12.2 versus 8.3), according to a simple calculation on the study's values. It does not say whether the same children fall behind as they get older, since the pupils compared are different. It suggests that childhood and adolescence weigh heavily, and therefore that this is where action is possible.

That leaves the question every reader asks: why?

Step 4 of 6

Why has endurance declined?

What is claimed: nobody has demonstrated it, but some overly simple explanations can be set aside. The studies measure the decline. They do not test its causes. There are, however, several clues, some of which point in unexpected directions.

Weight is not enough. In the international analysis, the link between the rise in overweight and the change in endurance is moderate before 2000 and negligible after. The French study, adjusted for BMI, still finds a decline.1,2 In Quebec, adjusting for body mass does not reduce the gap between 1982 and today either, and normal-weight girls have also fallen back.3 Overweight remains linked to poorer results in any given child: at 17, boys who are overweight or obese run clearly less well than the others.3 But it is not the only cause of the decline.

Physical activity poses a puzzle. The Quebec authors put forward a drop in activity and a rise in passive activities, without testing it.3 The national Esteban survey gives the picture in France: according to questionnaires completed by young people, 51% of boys and 33% of girls aged 6 to 17 meet the WHO recommendation, and the share drops after age 10.13

After age 10, the share of young people who move enough collapses

Values read in the report as fractions ("about 7 in 10", "1 in 2", "1 in 3", "1 in 5"), and therefore rounded. Activity reported by questionnaire, not measured by sensor; 1,182 children aged 6 to 17, mainland France, 2014-2016. Source: Santé publique France, Esteban.13

What this means

Adolescence is when the gap with the recommendation widens, especially in girls. This is consistent with the previous step, where the gap with 1982 is larger at age 17. This consistency proves nothing about the cause: the comparison is between different surveys.

The same report tempers the explanation based on sedentary behaviour: between 2006 and 2015, the share of young people meeting the recommendation did not change significantly, while daily screen time increased by about 25 minutes in 6-10 year-olds, 1 h 15 in 11-14 year-olds and nearly 2 hours in 15-17 year-olds.13 In the international analysis, the link between physical activity and the endurance trend has been weak since 2002.1

Inequalities are a lead. Across 18 countries, the Gini index (income inequality) is strongly and negatively associated with the endurance trend between 2000 and 2014: countries moving closer to equality have more favourable trends.1 This is a correlation between countries, which does not say by what mechanism. In France, ANSES notes that young people from the least advantaged backgrounds are more exposed to sedentary behaviour.14

What this means

The honest conclusion is "several leads, no hierarchy". Weight, activity, screens and inequalities are associated with endurance, but no study read here says in what proportions each plays a part. This matters for you: a child who runs less well should not be reduced to a single explanation.

If the causes remain unclear, what matters is whether the child's level counts for their future.

Step 5 of 6

Why it matters for what comes next

What is claimed: childhood endurance level partly carries over into adulthood, and it is associated with heart health later on. Two pieces of evidence are needed, and each has its limits.

The first concerns persistence. A review of 21 studies that followed 6,197 people for an average of 20.8 years finds a correlation of 0.38 (interval 0.29 to 0.48) between endurance in childhood or adolescence and in adulthood. The authors describe it as moderate, slightly stronger when starting from adolescence. The studies differ greatly from one another (heterogeneity of 92.7%).4 In practical terms, an enduring child is more likely to become an enduring adult, but childhood level explains only part of adult level: about 14%, from the square of 0.38 (a simple calculation, not a figure from the study). Nothing is settled, in either direction.

The second piece of evidence concerns health. A systematic review of 42 studies on cardiovascular risk concludes that there is strong evidence that a higher endurance level in childhood and adolescence is associated with a healthier cardiovascular profile later in life.7 Two large Swedish cohorts support this idea. Among 1,078,685 men assessed at about age 18 and followed for an average of 28.4 years, a high endurance level is associated with a markedly lower risk of disability pension for cardiovascular disease. For ischaemic heart disease, the risk ratio between the most and least enduring fifth is 0.11, or about 89% lower (a simple calculation).8 Among nearly 9,000 men, fitness at 18 goes with less atherosclerosis of the heart arteries nearly 40 years later, at about 50-64.9

What this means

A low endurance level at 10 or 17 is not a sentence, but it is a signal that goes along, at the scale of large groups, with a higher cardiovascular risk decades later. This is what justifies the interest in the decline in averages. But these two cohorts compare men with one another: they do not say that running more at 12 protects the heart at 55. This is the limit examined in the next step.

Step 6 of 6

And what if we are wrong? The objections

What is claimed: the links are real, but their size is probably overestimated. The main objection is this: fit teenagers may also be those with a favourable environment, better habits or better genes, and fitness may have almost nothing to do with it. A 2025 Swedish study tested this objection on about 1.1 million men, assessed at about age 18 between 1972 and 1995 and followed until their sixties. The usual result appears: the fittest group has a 58% lower risk of cardiovascular death, 31% for cancers and 53% for all causes. Then the authors looked at an event that fitness should not influence: deaths from accidents (car, drowning, homicide).10

The fittest also die less from accidents, which fitness does not explain

Swedish men assessed at about age 18, followed until their sixties; analyses adjusted for BMI, age, year, and parents' income and education. Scale: 4 px per percentage point. Source: Ballin et al., European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 2025 (Uppsala University press release).10

What this means

If fitness protected only through its effects on the heart, there would be no reason for it to reduce deaths from accidents by 53%. This result is a sign that a large part of the gap is due to other differences between fit men and the rest. The comparison between brothers, which removes part of these family differences, left the same result for accidents. The authors conclude that the protective effect is probably overestimated, without saying that exercise is useless. The study covers only men, measured once at age 18.

This study applies to the other figures in this article: the risk gaps in step 5 (0.11) and in the stakes (80%) are associations observed between groups of men or patients, which are better read as upper bounds than as effects of training.

Three other limits bear on the finding itself. First limit, measurement: field tests, equations and conditions vary, and the authors of the international analysis note that changes in biological maturation could lead to the true decline being underestimated, since recent children are on average more mature for a given age.1 Second limit, coverage: 15% of the world's population, mostly rich countries. Third limit, the figure that circulates: the loss of "25% in forty years" appears in none of the sources read for this article. The most complete international measurement gives 7.3% from 1981 to 2014. The "18.4% per decade" of the French study concerns test performance, with a different sample, and cannot be compared.1,2

What remains uncertain
  • The cause of the decline: weight, activity, screens and inequalities are leads, with no established hierarchy.
  • The real effect of a child's endurance on their health as an adult, once the other differences between families are set aside.
  • What happens outside rich countries and in girls during adolescence: data are scarcer.
  • What comes next: the decline has become very small, but the French authors ask for more data before concluding it is over.

Answer to the question

Let us return to the question asked at the start: has children's endurance declined, by how much, and does it change anything for their future? The answer comes in three levels of certainty.

Solid

Yes, it has declined. In 19 countries, mostly rich, the estimated endurance of 9-17 year-olds lost 7.3% from 1981 to 2014, more in boys than in girls, more in adolescence. In France, the decline was very strong between 1999 and 2010. It then almost stopped, without a return to the earlier level.

Probable

Childhood level partly carries over into adulthood (moderate correlation of 0.38), and a low level goes along with more cardiovascular risk decades later. These gaps are very probably overestimated in the raw figures.

Not demonstrated

That the average decline of 7% causes disease in the children concerned. That its cause is lifestyle rather than something else. That a specific child is affected: an average says nothing about an individual.

In plain terms, the alarm about a continuing collapse is not well founded. What is well founded: a lower starting level than before, which widens in adolescence, and a plausible link, but not proven as a cause, with future health. That is enough to act, because the useful actions are low-cost and recommended anyway for other reasons.

What to put in place

No study read here shows that a specific family programme raises a child's measured endurance. There are, however, school intervention trials and official recommendations. Here is what can be drawn from them, in order.

  1. Aim for 60 minutes a day on average.This is the WHO recommendation for ages 5-17: 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity per day on average over the week, mostly aerobic, with muscle-strengthening activities. It is rated as strong, with a moderate level of evidence. Walking to school, playing outside and doing sport all count.15
  2. Aim for regularity over several months.A meta-analysis of 40 studies (mostly randomised trials) on school programmes gives an average effect of 0.36 on children's endurance, described as small to moderate, with a low level of evidence. Programmes of at least 24 weeks and at least 3 sessions per week give larger effects than shorter ones (0.45 versus 0.28; 0.44 versus 0.26), but the authors present these differences as leads to be confirmed.16 Another meta-analysis of 43 studies on 27,626 children and adolescents finds an effect of 0.28.17
  3. Keep an eye on adolescence, especially in girls.This is where the share of sufficiently active young people drops and where the gap with 1982 is largest. ANSES recommends targeting 15-17 year-olds, modest backgrounds and adolescent girls, and varying activities (endurance, strength, flexibility), counting everyday movement.14
  4. Measure, without over-interpreting.The Fitness test on this page places your child against age and sex reference values. Repeat it under the same conditions (surface, time of day, warm-up), 3 to 6 months apart: this is an editorial choice, based on the fact that the gains from programmes appear within weeks and consolidate over months. A small difference from one attempt to the next may come from test error, not from training. Unusual breathlessness or chest pain warrants medical advice.

School programmes improve endurance, but the effect varies a lot from one programme to another

Meta-analysis of 40 studies (including 39 randomised trials), 32 studies and 17,880 children for endurance, children aged about 6 to 12; 95% confidence intervals. The bottom range is the prediction interval: in a future programme, the effect could be zero, or even slightly negative. Level of evidence judged low. Source: Frontiers in Public Health, 2026.16

What this means

Moving more, in class or outside it, improves a group of children's endurance on average, but the gain is modest and uneven. This is not a reason to do nothing: it is a reason to choose regular activities that the child wants to do again, and not to judge a programme after three sessions.

These actions do not depend on the exact cause of the decline. That is what allows them to be recommended despite the uncertainty.

What these studies do not show
  • They describe group averages. None of them characterises a particular child.
  • They mostly concern rich countries, with field tests under varying conditions.
  • They prove neither the causes of the decline, nor that this decline will cause disease.
  • The activity figures are reported by young people, not measured.

Frequently asked questions

Is the decline continuing?

In the countries studied, it has become negligible since the 2000s, and very small in France since 2010.1,2 None of the studies read shows a clear recovery, and the French authors ask for more data to confirm the slowdown.

Is my child affected?

An average is not an individual, and the shuttle run is too imprecise to judge a single child. A test, compared with age and sex reference values, then repeated under the same conditions, is the only way to place them.

Should screens be limited to protect endurance?

Nothing in the studies read directly links screen time to endurance. ANSES uses a reference point of 2 hours a day of leisure screen time beyond which a health risk may exist, and proposes replacing some screen time with activity. The WHO considers that the evidence is not sufficient to set a precise threshold.14,15 The 2-hour reference point is cautious, not demonstrated.

You read that young people have lost 25% of their cardiovascular capacity in 40 years. Is that correct?

No open source for this article allows it to be confirmed. The most complete international measurement gives a 7.3% decline from 1981 to 2014.1 The 25% figure is therefore not used here.
